t: 3645 — Maximum Total from Optimal Activation Order
o: Activating element i requires the current active count to be strictly below limit[i]; afterwards, once the active count reaches x, every element with limit ≤ x dies permanently. Since the active count grows by exactly 1 per activation, an element activated at step i (1-indexed) needs limit ≥ i. So a set is activatable in some order iff, sorted by limit ascending, the i-th smallest limit is ≥ i. All values are positive, so we want the largest activatable set.
k: Activation step i requires limit ≥ i, so sort by limit and greedily take elements while limit > current active count.
Skipping a too-small-limit element never hurts: all later candidates have ≥ limits, and values are positive so taking everything feasible is optimal.
One pass after sorting suffices — O(n log n).

a.n: Approach 1: Sort by limit + greedy admission
a.i: Sort elements by limit ascending. Sweep with a counter of active elements; admit an element iff its limit strictly exceeds the current count (meaning it can occupy the next activation slot). An element whose limit is too small now can never be activated later since the count only grows, and excluding it doesn't relax constraints for others (they have larger or equal limits). Every admitted element adds its value.
s: Pair up (limit, value) and sort by limit ascending.
For each pair in order: if limit > active, total += value, active += 1.
a.t: O(n log n) — sorting dominates; the sweep is linear

w: Exchange argument for optimality: if a feasible schedule activates a set S, sorting S by limit and activating in that order works (the i-th activated has the i-th smallest limit, which must be ≥ i since at most limit−1 elements precede it). Hence max total = max sum over prefix-feasible sets, which the greedy achieves. Pitfalls: using >= instead of strict > for the limit check, and 32-bit overflow on the total (up to 1e10) in C++/Java. Follow-up: if values could be negative you'd need a heap-based selection instead.
